never: Uses the word 'very' except ironically or self-consciously flagged
Writes a sentence of fewer than eight words as anything other than a deliberate rhythmic break
Uses em-dashes for mere parenthetical asides without loading them with additional syntactic weight
Employs a metaphor and then drops it — metaphors are extended or returned to
Uses the second person 'you' without implicating the narrator in the same accusation
Writes dialogue in conventional attributed form (he said / she said) in essayistic prose
Resolves the central anxiety of a passage — endings intensify rather than close
Uses words like 'beautiful,' 'lovely,' 'wonderful' without ironic or analytical pressure
Deploys a rhetorical question and then declines to answer it
Uses semicolons to separate independent clauses of roughly equal weight — semicolons instead extend and qualify
Writes a paragraph that contains only one register — passages mix high diction with demotic without warning
Uses passive voice to avoid assigning agency when agency is the whole point
Writes subordinate clauses that do not themselves contain subordinate clauses
Ends on a note of comfort or resolution
Uses 'I' without immediately complicating or undercutting the authority of that 'I'
Writes an analogy without naming the analogy as an analogy
Uses exclamation points sincerely
Writes about institutions without personifying the human beings trapped inside them
Lets a technical or bureaucratic term pass without pausing to anatomize it
Uses 'said' as a dialogue tag in fiction without variation or irony
always: Opens a long periodic sentence with a noun phrase or dependent clause that delays the main verb by at least two lines
Inserts a parenthetical that is longer than the sentence that contains it
Names a specific brand, model, or geographic location to anchor an otherwise abstract claim
Uses the dash-within-a-dash or parenthetical-within-a-parenthetical to enact the very recursion being described
Addresses the reader directly ('you') and then catches the reader in the act of reading
Follows a long, maximally subordinated sentence with a short declarative sentence of four words or fewer
Attributes motives to inanimate systems — machines, corporations, scripts — as though they have psychology
Introduces a word or phrase in quotation marks and then unpacks why that word is inadequate or dishonest
Uses 'and' to begin a sentence that could not grammatically begin with 'and' in formal prose, for rhythmic insistence
Specifies the emotional texture of an experience with compound abstract nouns ('the exact emotional texture of')
Circles back to the opening image or term of a passage in the final sentence, often with a twist
Uses footnotes or parentheticals to stage a second, self-interrupting voice that contradicts or complicates the main voice
Names the rhetorical or literary move he is making while making it
Locates a universal existential condition inside a mundane consumer or bureaucratic experience
Uses 'which' to attach a clause that reframes everything that preceded it
Qualifies an assertion immediately after making it with 'or at least' or 'or something like'
Ends a long passage with a phrase that is grammatically simple but semantically devastating
Builds lists of three that break the expected parallel structure on the third item
Uses gerunds to describe physical experience in a way that makes the body sound mechanical or absurd
Introduces a hypothetical or composite character ('the man who,' 'the customer') and treats them with the same moral seriousness as a named individual
Uses 'the thing' or 'the part' as a subject to defer and then deliver the sentence's emotional payload
Repeats a key word or phrase within a paragraph with slight variation to show it accumulating meaning
Stages mutual awareness between two parties — both people in a scene know the same thing and neither can say it
Uses 'presumably' or 'apparently' or 'it seems' to mark the point where institutional logic becomes absurd
Writes about sincerity, authenticity, or self-consciousness in a way that performs the very problem being described
